jurisdiction.name: PIPEDA
jurisdiction.fullName: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act

authority.name: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada

articles.surfaceLabel: Does Canada's Federal Privacy Law Apply to Your Business?
articles.plainSummary: PIPEDA covers businesses that handle personal information in commercial activity across most of Canada. Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia have their own private-sector laws for activity inside those provinces.
articles.personalImpact: In 2022, regulators found the Tim Hortons app tracked people's location even when it was closed. In 2023, a breach at 23andMe exposed the genetic data of about 320,000 Canadians. In 2025 the UK fined the company, but Canada's regulator could not. PIPEDA sets your rights, yet its enforcement still relies mostly on recommendations and the courts.
articles.professionalLayer: PIPEDA applies to organizations that collect, use or disclose personal information in the course of commercial activities, and to federally regulated employers for their staff data. It has no size threshold. Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia have private-sector laws the federal government has declared substantially similar, and those apply instead for activity inside each province. PIPEDA still applies there to federally regulated businesses and to information crossing provincial or national borders. Ontario, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Nova Scotia have similar laws for health information. Federal government institutions fall under the separate Privacy Act. Courts apply PIPEDA to foreign organizations with a real and substantial connection to Canada. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner investigates complaints and can enter enforceable compliance agreements, but it cannot issue orders or fines. After a complaint, individuals can go to the Federal Court, which can order changes and award damages. Knowing breaches of key duties, such as breach reporting, are offences with fines up to C$100,000. The EU recognises PIPEDA as adequate for commercial organizations. A bill introduced in June 2026, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, would replace PIPEDA's privacy rules, but it is not law. A 2026 amendment adding a data mobility right has passed but is not yet in force.

sourceLinks.label: Provincial laws that may apply instead: OPC

articles.assessTrigger: Do you handle personal information of people in Canada in commercial activity, and have you checked whether a provincial law applies instead for Quebec, Alberta or British Columbia?

gapRemediation.smb: Map where your customers and staff are. PIPEDA applies regardless of size, and Quebec adds its own stricter rules.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Treat Quebec as a separate track. Its law adds impact assessments, express consent for sensitive data, and administrative penalties.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Run a Canada program covering PIPEDA, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia, and track the federal reform bill.

comparisonFlags.note: The federal regulator cannot fine. Enforcement runs through recommendations, compliance agreements and the Federal Court.

articles.surfaceLabel: When Businesses Need Your Consent in Canada
articles.plainSummary: Canadian businesses generally need your consent to collect, use or share your personal information. The form of consent depends on how sensitive the information is, with listed exceptions.
articles.personalImpact: Apps often bury sweeping permissions in long terms. PIPEDA says consent only counts if you could reasonably understand what you agreed to. A business also cannot demand consent beyond what its service needs. Uses a reasonable person would find inappropriate are not allowed at all.
articles.professionalLayer: PIPEDA is built on ten principles in Schedule 1, with consent as the default. Consent is valid only if the people it targets would reasonably understand the nature, purpose and consequences of the collection, use or disclosure. Organizations should generally seek express consent for sensitive information, and implied consent can suit less sensitive information within reasonable expectations. A business cannot make consent a condition of service beyond what the stated, legitimate purpose needs. People can withdraw consent at any time, subject to legal or contractual limits and reasonable notice. Separately, any purpose must be one a reasonable person would consider appropriate, even with consent. Section 7 lists closed exceptions for collection, use and disclosure without consent, such as emergencies, legal requirements, investigations and debt collection. Business transactions and federally regulated employment relationships have their own exceptions. There is no contract or legitimate-interests basis.

sourceLinks.label: Guidelines for obtaining meaningful consent: OPC

articles.assessTrigger: Is each use of Canadian personal information backed by meaningful consent in the right form, or by a listed exception, and would a reasonable person find the purpose appropriate?

gapRemediation.smb: Explain uses in plain words at sign-up, and ask for express consent for anything sensitive.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Review uses justified elsewhere by contract or legitimate interests. In Canada they need consent or a listed exception.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Follow the regulator's seven consent principles, and record why each use passes the reasonable-person test.

comparisonFlags.note: PIPEDA is consent-centred with closed exceptions. It has no contract or legitimate-interests basis.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to See Your Information
articles.plainSummary: You can ask a business whether it holds personal information about you, see it, and learn how it was used and who received it. It must answer within 30 days.
articles.personalImpact: Loyalty programs, banks and apps build files about you over years. What they hold, and who they shared it with, is usually invisible. This right lets you ask to see it all. A hidden file becomes something you can check.
articles.professionalLayer: Principle 4.9 requires an organization, on request, to say whether it holds personal information about the person, give access, and account for its uses and the third parties that received it. Requests are made in writing, and the organization must help the requester. It must respond within 30 days of receipt. It can extend this by up to 30 more days if meeting the deadline would unreasonably interfere with its activities, or if it needs to consult others, and longer to convert the information into an alternative format. It must give notice of any extension within the first 30 days. Access must be at minimal or no cost, with advance notice of any fee. Refusals must be in writing, with reasons and the person's options for recourse.
articles.responseTimeline: 30 days from receipt. Extendable by up to 30 more days with notice, or longer for alternative formats.
articles.assessTrigger: Can you answer Canadian access requests within 30 days, including how the information was used and which third parties received it?

gapRemediation.smb: Keep a simple log of who you share data with, so access answers can include it.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Build the 30-day clock and the extension notice into your request workflow.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Automate access packages that include disclosure history, and record the reasons for any refusal.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Correct Your Information
articles.plainSummary: If information about you is inaccurate or incomplete, the business must correct it and, where appropriate, tell others who received it. There is no general right to have data deleted on request.
articles.personalImpact: A wrong entry in a credit or customer file can follow you for years. It can cost you a loan or a fair price. This right lets you have inaccurate information fixed or removed. Where a dispute remains, your side must be recorded.
articles.professionalLayer: When a person shows that information is inaccurate or incomplete, the organization must amend it by correcting, deleting or adding information. Where appropriate, it must pass the change to third parties that have the information. If a challenge is not resolved, the organization must record it and, where appropriate, tell those third parties. PIPEDA has no general right to erasure. Information no longer needed for its purposes should be destroyed, erased or made anonymous, and withdrawing consent can lead to deletion. Quebec's law goes further: it gives a right to deletion where keeping the data is not authorized by law, and a right to have certain information de-indexed.
articles.responseTimeline: PIPEDA's 30-day deadline covers requests under the access principle, which includes correction.
articles.assessTrigger: Can you correct records, pass corrections to third parties, record unresolved disputes, and destroy data you no longer need?

gapRemediation.smb: Set retention periods and delete data once its purpose is done.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Add correction notices to third parties and dispute notes to your workflow.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Handle Quebec deletion and de-indexing requests on a separate track from PIPEDA corrections.

articles.surfaceLabel: What Happens When Your Data Is Breached
articles.plainSummary: If a breach creates a real risk of significant harm, the business must report it to the federal regulator and notify affected people as soon as feasible. It must keep a record of every breach.
articles.personalImpact: A breach can expose your bank details, health data or account passwords. Silence gives fraudsters a head start. PIPEDA requires the business to warn you when the risk of harm is real. You learn in time to protect yourself.
articles.professionalLayer: Mandatory breach notification began in November 2018. An organization must report a breach of security safeguards to the Privacy Commissioner, and notify affected individuals, where it is reasonable to believe the breach creates a real risk of significant harm. Significant harm includes humiliation, reputational damage, financial loss, identity theft and damage to credit. The test weighs how sensitive the information is and how likely it is to be misused. Both notices are due as soon as feasible after the organization determines the breach occurred, with no fixed hour count. Notices to individuals must be direct unless that would cause further harm or undue hardship. Organizations must also tell other bodies that can reduce the harm. They must keep a record of every breach, notifiable or not, for 24 months and show it to the regulator on request. Knowingly failing to report, notify or keep records is an offence with fines up to C$100,000.
articles.responseTimeline: Regulator and individuals: as soon as feasible where there is a real risk of significant harm. Breach records kept for 24 months.

sourceLinks.label: Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations: Justice Laws

articles.assessTrigger: Does your incident plan apply the real-risk-of-significant-harm test, and do you keep a record of every breach for 24 months?

gapRemediation.smb: Keep a breach log for every incident, even small ones, for at least 24 months.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Write down how you assess the risk of significant harm, so the reasoning is on record.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Run Canadian federal and Quebec notices side by side. Quebec requires prompt notice and its own incident register.

comparisonFlags.note: Canada uses a real-risk-of-significant-harm test and an as-soon-as-feasible duty, not a 72-hour clock.

articles.plainSummary: Canada has no list of approved countries. A business that sends your information abroad stays responsible for it and must protect it by contract. It must also tell you it may be processed in other countries.
articles.personalImpact: Many Canadian services store data on servers in other countries. There, foreign courts and authorities may be able to reach it. PIPEDA keeps the Canadian business accountable wherever your data goes. You must be told that it may leave the country.
articles.professionalLayer: PIPEDA has no transfer-specific rules, adequacy list, standard clauses or certification scheme. Under the accountability principle, an organization stays responsible for information it transfers to a third party for processing. It must use contractual or other means to provide a comparable level of protection. The regulator treats a transfer for processing as a use, not a disclosure, so it needs no separate consent. It does need openness: people should be told their information may be processed abroad and reached by foreign authorities. The regulator considered requiring consent for transfers in 2019 but kept its existing guidance. Quebec is stricter: before communicating personal information outside Quebec, an organization must assess the privacy impact and may proceed only if protection would be adequate, under a written agreement.

sourceLinks.label: Guidelines for processing personal data across borders: OPC

articles.assessTrigger: Do your contracts give comparable protection to Canadian data processed abroad, and does your privacy notice say it may leave Canada?

gapRemediation.smb: Add privacy and security terms to contracts with foreign providers, and mention foreign processing in your privacy notice.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Keep a list of where Canadian data is processed and the contract that protects each flow.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Run Quebec transfer impact assessments before data leaves the province, alongside federal accountability.

comparisonFlags.note: Canada relies on organizational accountability rather than country approvals or standard clauses.
